top.line: A broken written prohibition should shift liability to vendors
top.para: Ralf Thomas asked why AI agents should differ from employees whose damage the company pays for. The accountability shell game works because nothing was written down between clicking allow and the failure. My hypothesis is that an explicit prohibition the agent breaks moves liability towards the platform, so every looping agent needs a behaviour policy.

in-short.line: The shell game works because nothing was written down
in-short.para: Agent companies answered 2026's failures by blaming the agent, the customer, the contract, or disclosing late. A behaviour policy writes down explicit prohibitions. Towards the world the deployer still answers, but between deployer and vendor a broken written rule turns user error into product defect, as EU product liability covers software from 9 December 2026.

post.line: The post's 2026 record is mostly right, with corrections
post.para: Codex deleting home directories, an OpenAI evaluation agent breaching Hugging Face, Anthropic's evaluation models reaching real systems and Amazon's user-error statement on Kiro support the four-move pattern. But the Air Canada quote was the tribunal's summary, Garcia and Mobley were motion-to-dismiss rulings, and Microsoft removed its entertainment-only Copilot wording.

why.line: Without a written mandate, every deflection is unanswerable
why.para: An agent has a reach and a mandate, and the gap is the risk. When only a system prompt stood between full access and the failure, the vendor can fairly say the customer granted the reach. Without the mandate written down, neither 'an honest mistake' nor 'the customer allowed it' can be answered.

line.line: Written prohibitions are still hope, but on the record
line.para: My own agents are told not to send email directly, edit others' files, change scheduled tasks, attack sites or speak on my behalf; businesses add rules like making no offers. Most are expectations enforced by nobody, and my agent broke one on 9 October. Yet a written, broken rule changes a dispute fundamentally.

liability.line: A product breaking an accepted rule looks defective
liability.para: Liability towards the world starts with whoever granted the reach, as the Air Canada tribunal held, while vendor terms put all actions on the customer, defensible only when the customer said nothing. The EU Product Liability Directive treats software as a product from 9 December 2026, and Germany's Bundestag passed its version on 8 October.

direction.line: Every looping agent needs a policy beside its prompt
direction.para: Any agent with Simon Willison's lethal trifecta should not run on a prompt alone. Claude Code's permission rules and Codex's approval modes enforce some rows, but there is no place for business rules. Vendors should accept the policy, enforce what they can, log and disclose breaches, and own broken rows.

limits.line: This is a hypothesis about disputes, not settled law
limits.para: It is not legal advice and no court has decided the question; Garcia, Mobley and Moffatt were early or small-claims rulings. The product liability rules cover only death, injury, property damage and data loss. A written policy does not make the agent comply, and the article refines the earlier claim that liability always sits with the customer.

sources.line: Sources: the incident reports, cases and laws cited
sources.para: The article came from my voice memo of 13 October 2026 responding to Ralf Thomas's post. Sources include The Register, Hugging Face's incident disclosure, Anthropic's investigation and alignment assessment, Amazon's Kiro statement, Moffatt v. Air Canada, the Product Liability Directive, the Bundestag debate, Anthropic's terms, Claude Code permissions and Simon Willison's lethal trifecta.
